Amoz
ā'mŏz
n. (the father of Isaiah the prophet — named in the superscription of the greatest of the prophetic books and nowhere else described)
From Hebrew 'Amots, strong, from 'amats, to be strong or courageous. He is not to be confused with the prophet Amos, whose name is a different Hebrew word, 'Amos, a burden-bearer.

Biblical Definition

Amoz is known by one relationship. Thirteen times Scripture calls the prophet “Isaiah the son of Amoz”, and nothing else is recorded of the man — not his tribe, not his trade, not a word he spoke. He opens the book: “The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah” (Isa 1:1), and heads the major sections after it (Isa 2:1; Isa 13:1). When Hezekiah sends his officers in sackcloth in the worst hour of the Assyrian siege, they are sent “to Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz” (2Ki 19:2), the patronymic still attached at the crisis of the kingdom. Jewish tradition, which the dictionary reports without endorsing, makes Amoz a brother of king Amaziah and so places Isaiah in the royal family, which would explain the prophet's access to kings and his command of court and diplomatic language. Scripture does not say so. What Scripture does is fix a name in the superscription of sixty-six chapters, so that the book announces itself as the vision of a particular man, son of a particular father, in the reigns of four named kings — a prophecy with an address, not an anonymous oracle.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Amoz; in sacred history he is the father of the prophet Isaiah, distinguished from Amos the herdman of Tekoa.

expand to see more

AMOZ, n. The father of Isaiah the prophet; the name signifies strong.

He is named only in the title of the prophecy and in the books of Kings and Chronicles.

He is not the same with Amos, the herdman of Tekoa, whose name is written differently in the Hebrew.

The Jewish writers make him the brother of Amaziah, king of Judah, but this rests on tradition only.

The repeated designation Isaiah the son of Amoz distinguishes the prophet in the sacred records.

Key Scripture

Isa 1:1 — "The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah."

Isa 2:1 — "The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem."

Isa 13:1 — "The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see."

2Ki 19:2 — "And he sent Eliakim, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the elders of the priests, covered with sackcloth, to Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz."

Modern Corruption

The recurring superscription “Isaiah the son of Amoz” is the book's own claim to a single eighth-century author; the division of Isaiah into two or three prophets is asserted against it.

expand to see more

The critical division of Isaiah into a first prophet of the eighth century and one or two later writers is the standard position of the academy, and the reason offered is that chapters 40 and following address the exile as a present reality and name Cyrus, who was not born. That reasoning excludes predictive prophecy before examining the text, which is a philosophical commitment rather than a finding. The book itself names one author in three superscriptions, always as the son of Amoz. The New Testament quotes from both halves and attributes both to the same man — in one passage John cites chapter 53 and chapter 6 in consecutive verses and says “Esaias said again” (Joh 12:39-41). The Lord Jesus in the synagogue at Nazareth was handed “the book of the prophet Esaias” (Luk 4:17) and read chapter 61 from it. The dictionary holds one Isaiah, and holds it on the authority of the Lord who read him.

The second thing to say about Amoz is pastoral. He is a name and a fatherhood, with no recorded words. Most Christian men will be that: not the prophet, but the father of one; not the reformer, but the household in which a reformer was catechised. Scripture's way of honouring such men is not to write their biographies but to keep their names permanently attached to what their children did. Thirteen times, across three books and seven centuries of transmission, someone had to write “the son of Amoz.”

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Amots (H531), Amoz, from 'amats (H553), to be strong, alert, courageous; distinct from 'Amos (H5986).

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Amots (H531) — Amoz, “strong”; the father of Isaiah.

Hebrew 'amats (H553) — to be strong, to confirm; the word of Jos 1:9, “be strong and of a good courage”.

Hebrew 'Amos (H5986) — Amos, a burden-bearer; a different name and a different man, the herdman of Tekoa.

Hebrew Yesha'yahu (H3470) — Isaiah, “the salvation of the LORD”; the theme of the whole book in the prophet's name.

Hebrew chazon (H2377) — a vision; the word that opens the book (Isa 1:1).

Usage

"“The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz” — a prophecy with an author and an address."

"“The burden of Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz did see” — the same name over the later oracles."

"“To Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz” — the patronymic still attached in the siege."
